editor: Curated daily for Wits AHEAD. Every item is checked against its source before it is listed. Summaries are the group's own; follow the link for the original.

items.title: University of Leicester gives Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 21,000 students and 4,000 staff
items.summary: From September 2026 every student and staff member at Leicester has full Copilot access across Microsoft 365, paired with mandatory digital-skills modules completed in Blackboard before access opens. Manchester announced a similar whole-institution rollout in January.
items.why: Whole-institution AI provision changes the baseline for academic integrity, assessment design and equity of access. It is a live test case for Pillar 1 and a benchmark South African universities will be measured against.

items.title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence
items.summary: The Bank's first dedicated assessment of AI for low- and middle-income countries, framed as adopt, adapt, advance. Middle-income countries made up half of ChatGPT's traffic within six months of launch, faster diffusion than any earlier general-purpose technology, yet the report sets out the electricity, connectivity and data conditions that must be met before AI improves public services.
items.why: The report is the policy frame funders will use for the next five years. AHEAD's Global South, capability-first stance is a direct response to its adopt-adapt-advance agenda.

items.title: Youth unemployment (15 to 34) rises to 47.4% in the second quarter of 2026
items.source: Statistics South Africa, Quarterly Labour Force Survey Q2 2026
items.summary: The official youth unemployment rate increased by 1.5 percentage points to 47.4% in Q2 2026. Unemployed youth rose by 264,000 to 5.0 million while employed youth fell by 40,000 to 5.6 million.
items.why: This is the single defensible figure the group uses for graduate pathways and just transitions. Pillar 4 asks how AI reshapes the route from qualification to livelihood for exactly this cohort.

items.title: UC Berkeley Law bans generative AI on all graded work from Summer 2026
items.source: UC Berkeley School of Law policy; reported in Forbes
items.summary: Students may not use generative AI to conceptualise, outline, draft, revise, translate or edit graded work, nor in any exam, and may not upload course materials into AI systems. The trigger was a measurable spike in hallucinated citations and flawed analysis in submissions.
items.why: The opposite pole to Leicester. Together they bracket the design space for assessment and integrity policy that Pillar 1 studies, and they show why evidence, not instinct, should decide.

items.title: Student Generative AI Survey 2026: 95% of undergraduates now use AI for academic work
items.source: Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI) and Kortext
items.summary: Use rose from 66% in 2024 to 92% in 2025 and 95% in 2026, but use to generate text fell from 64% to 56%. Institutional provision of AI tools rose to 38% of students, from 9% two years earlier. Concerns about fairness and skill erosion persist.
items.why: A three-year longitudinal series is exactly the evidence base Pillar 1 lacks in South Africa. It is the model for the national student survey the group should run.

items.title: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026: generative AI improves performance without guaranteeing learning
items.summary: The Outlook reviews generative AI used by students alone, by students and teachers together, and by teachers alone. Intelligent tutoring can scale personalised learning, including in low-infrastructure settings, but over-reliance on tools that give direct answers reduces engagement and yields performance gains without learning gains.
items.why: The performance-versus-learning distinction is the core measurement problem for Pillars 1 and 2, and it maps onto the capability approach: what students can actually do, not what their outputs look like.

items.title: Digitalisation and the use of AI in African higher education: UNESCO-ICHEI exploratory study released
items.source: UNESCO International Centre for Higher Education Innovation (ICHEI)
items.summary: The study maps digitalisation and AI adoption across sub-Saharan African universities and finds ambition running ahead of infrastructure, governance and staff capacity.
items.why: The clearest recent evidence of the gap AHEAD exists to fill: a Global South-anchored research entity that treats AI in higher education as its object and method.

items.title: From engagement to outcomes: AI-driven learning analytics in higher education, insights for South Africa
items.summary: Reviews the move from dashboards to deep-learning early-alert systems that combine behavioural, cognitive and affective indicators, with cases from UNISA (risk profiling and progression dashboards) and the University of Pretoria (analytics-enabled advising and gateway-course redesign). Adoption is held back by fragmented data systems, weak interoperability, low data literacy and ethical concerns.
items.why: Pillar 2 in one paper: the South African state of the art in predictive analytics for retention, and the barriers a research group can help remove.

items.title: Reframing AI and learning analytics in emerging higher education: towards a human-centred, contextually responsive future
items.source: Frontiers in Education, peer-reviewed scoping review
items.summary: A critical scoping review of 31 studies (2019 to 2026) on AI and learning analytics implementation across Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and the Middle East, arguing for human-centred, context-responsive design over imported models.
items.why: The review's Global South frame and its human-centred thesis are AHEAD's own. It is a reference point for the group's positioning papers and a map of collaborators.

items.title: The impact of AI on work in higher education
items.summary: EDUCAUSE surveys how AI is changing academic and professional work inside universities: which tasks are being automated, where staff want support, and how institutions are governing use.
items.why: Pillar 5 is about evidence for institutional decision-making. This is the kind of instrument the group can adapt for South African universities.

items.title: 2026 Future of Jobs Summit puts AI reskilling at the centre of South Africa's employment debate
items.summary: Business, technology and youth leaders called for urgent collaboration, digital infrastructure investment and AI-driven reskilling, and described the T-shaped graduate employers now seek: deep expertise plus AI literacy, data analytics and ethical judgement.
items.why: Employers are redefining employability in real time. Pillar 4 reframes that demand as capability for work and life, not only a skills list.

items.title: AI in Africa's universities: bridging the gap between promise and readiness
items.summary: African universities are exploring AI's potential while ambition outpaces infrastructure, governance and faculty capacity; the piece surveys institutional responses across the continent.
items.why: Context for the group's differentiation line: concentration on AI as research object and method is what most African universities still lack.

items.title: Still emerging: understanding generative AI use in higher education
items.summary: An empirical study of how students and academics are actually using generative AI, finding practice still unsettled and unevenly supported by institutions.
items.why: Useful comparator for the group's own bibliometric and survey work under Pillar 1.

items.title: Open dataset: anonymised records of information systems students at a South African university for learning analytics
items.summary: A de-identified student dataset released for learning-analytics research, one of very few open South African datasets of its kind.
items.why: Open, local data is the scarcest input for Pillar 2. This is a candidate training and benchmarking set for the group's early-warning work.

items.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
items.summary: The second edition of the independent international synthesis of evidence on general-purpose AI capabilities, risks and mitigations.
items.why: Pillar 6 draws its risk vocabulary from here. Essential background for responsible-AI policy in Global South higher education.

items.title: Are graduates prepared for the AI era?
items.summary: Working It editor Isabel Berwick looks at how institutions worldwide are helping graduates into first jobs, and the tools and skills that now drive a successful search.
items.why: The graduate-transition question of Pillar 4, told from the employer and graduate side.

items.title: Reinventing teaching after the introduction of AI
items.source: TEDx Talks, Prof. Amy Bruckman (Georgia Tech)
items.credibility: TEDx; Regents' Professor, Georgia Institute of Technology
items.summary: A computing professor on what teaching is for when AI can do the assignments, drawing on years in the classroom.
items.why: A clear statement of the pedagogical redesign problem at the heart of Pillar 1.

items.title: How AI will change education, according to Harvard's President
items.source: The 92nd Street Y, New York, with Alan Garber
items.summary: Alan Garber on why the real challenge is not what AI can do but what humans must learn to do better.
items.why: A capability argument from the top of the sector: the question is human development, not tool adoption.

items.title: 'AI is changing everything' in higher education, says Georgia Tech's President
items.credibility: Bloomberg; President, Georgia Institute of Technology
items.summary: Ángel Cabrera on the outlook for higher education amid economic uncertainty and how AI is changing how students learn.
items.why: Institutional strategy under AI, the decision-making layer Pillar 5 serves with evidence.

items.title: 'Don't walk alone': Prof. Mwenda Ntarangwi on collaboration, AI and the future of African higher education
items.source: The Education Collaborative, with the Vice-Chancellor of USIU-Africa
items.summary: Recorded at the Collaborative's Kigali convening ahead of its Nairobi East Africa Hub meeting in October 2026: collaboration, hub progress and technology's role in African higher education.
items.why: African leadership on exactly the collaborative, cross-institution model AHEAD is built on.

items.title: Nigeria's AI education revolution: how AI is reshaping learning, from the University of Lagos
items.summary: Education experts at UNILAG on how AI is shaping classrooms and academic work, and the call for guidance, regulation and responsible use.
items.why: From a partner institution on the group's footprint, and squarely on Pillar 6.

items.title: Development as Freedom
items.summary: The capability approach in its original statement: development as the expansion of the real freedoms people have reason to value.
items.why: The H in AHEAD. Start here.

items.title: Professional Education, Capabilities and the Public Good: the role of universities in promoting human development
items.source: Melanie Walker and Monica McLean, Routledge (2013)
items.credibility: Peer-reviewed monograph, South African research base
items.summary: The capability approach translated into higher education, built on South African case studies of professional education.
items.why: The bridge from Sen to universities, written from this country.

items.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
items.summary: The first global guidance on generative AI in education: human agency, inclusion, equity, age limits, data protection and teacher capacity.
items.why: The policy baseline for Pillar 6 and for any South African institutional policy.

items.title: Data Feminism
items.source: Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren F. Klein, MIT Press (2020), open access
items.summary: Seven principles for data science that examines power and works toward justice.
items.why: The data-justice grounding for analytics that reduce rather than reproduce inequality.

items.title: Algorithmic injustice: a relational ethics approach
items.summary: Why fairness cannot be fixed technically alone: a relational ethics for algorithmic systems, from an African scholar.
items.why: The decolonial-computing thread in the group's theoretical spine.
